c: When starting is the hard part

A prompt, shared start time, visible next action or easier task environment can reduce friction. None is guaranteed, and effectiveness should be judged by whether the person’s function improves without an unsustainable effort cost.
“One failed tip means the person has not tried.” A visible result cannot, on its own, explain the process behind it.

c: Illustration of lived experience, not a biological mechanism

Many people describe a gap between deciding to do something and doing it. This drawing is a metaphor for that experience: the intention is there, but getting it through to action takes extra effort and arrives late. It is not a picture of brain activity, a transmitter level or a diagnosis, and it does not explain why the gap happens for any one person. For the biology that is actually established, see

Run a short personal trial and keep only what actually helps.

This page is general information. Personal experience varies. A source supporting a clinical framework does not automatically validate every suggested coping technique or prove an individual causal mechanism. Claims are dated, jurisdiction-limited where relevant, and should be corrected when stronger evidence changes the conclusion.

Prompts, shared starts and environmental changes can reduce task friction, but they are not substitutes for clinical care. If medication or another established treatment changes or stops, practical coping tools should sit alongside an appropriate medical review rather than being presented as a replacement for it.
If there is immediate risk, use the appropriate urgent or emergency route. For a non-emergency continuity problem, the useful question is who owns the next clinical decision and when it will be made.
